title: Neural network support: multi-output networks (trunk/heads, keras functional API)
description:
Follow-on from #149. Milestones 1-3 of the neural network support work (bare torch, `parsnip::mlp(engine = "brulee")`, and bare keras3 `Sequential`, all feed-forward and fully-connected) are merged. This tracks Milestone 5 from the dev plan: multi-output network support. Scoped separately rather than as a subtask of #149 because it touches shared code every existing model goes through (`check_mode()`, `set_pred_names()`) and has no driving use case yet.

## Scope

- Torch: explicit `list(trunk = ..., heads = list(...))` input shape, reusing the existing walker once per trunk/head.
- Keras: extend the keras walker to also accept `keras.src.models.functional.Functional`, walking `get_config()$layers`' `inbound_nodes`/`keras_history` into a small dependency graph.
- Package-wide ripple: `type`/`lvl`/`prefix` accept a named-list-keyed-by-head form in addition to their existing single-value form (with an explicit early error if the shape doesn't match what the model needs); `set_pred_names()` loops per head with head names woven into output column names to prevent collisions; `check_mode()`/`check_type()` run per-head instead of assuming one mode per object.
- Tests: mixed-mode object (one regression head, one classification head) end to end through `predict()`, `orbital_sql()`, and `orbital_dt()`.

**Explicitly out of scope even within this milestone:** torch models with genuinely arbitrary custom `forward()` methods (needs `torch::jit_trace()`-based graph extraction, a materially larger project).

**Size:** L-XL, mostly because of the shared-code-path changes rather than the extraction logic itself, which reuses the existing walkers directly. Given the size, likely deserves a similar torch/keras PR split the way the torch+brulee work did.

title: orbital:::orbital.step_mutate() Cannot Encode Longer Expressions
description:
Hey there! Thanks so much for all of the work on `orbital`, its an awesome package. For governance reasons, we are very explicit with preprocessing logic in `recipes::step_mutate()` often taking plain fields and encoding them as bins or other categorical variables.

In the example below, you can see where shorter `dplyr::case_when()` statements are represented by `orbital` just fine. However, longer expressions are truncated to `...` for brevity which results in information loss when the `orbital` object is used for inference later.

As far as I can tell, this is because `orbital:::orbital.step_mutate()` uses `rlang::as_label()` which ends up truncating longer expressions. I cloned the `orbital` main branch at 3b0a164 and modified the function to the following and it works great. I reran `test-step_mutate.R` and they passed.

```r
orbital.step_mutate <- function(x, all_vars, ...) {
  input <- x$input

  input <- input[names(input) %in% all_vars]

  out <- vapply(
    input,
    \(expr) rlang::expr_text(rlang::quo_squash(expr)),
    character(1)
  )
  names(out) <- names(input)
  out
}
```

## Reproducible example

```r
#### Setup ####

library(orbital)
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)

train <- ggplot2::diamonds

#### Simple Model ####

model_simple <-
  recipes::recipe(
    price ~ .,
    data = head(train, 0)
  ) |>
  recipes::update_role(
    new_role = "metadata",
    recipes::all_predictors()
  ) |>
  recipes::step_mutate(
    # rlang::as_label() works here and converts this
    # dplyr::case_when() statement to a working expression
    carat_bin = dplyr::case_when(
      carat <= 0.25 ~ "low",
      carat > 0.25 ~ "high"
    ),
    carat_bin = factor(carat_bin, c("low", "high"))
  ) |>
  recipes::step_dummy(carat_bin) |>
  workflows::workflow(
    spec = parsnip::linear_reg()
  ) |>
  parsnip::fit(train)

orbital::orbital(model_simple) |>
  parsnip::augment(train)
#> # A tibble: 53,940 × 11
#>    .pred carat cut       color clarity depth table price     x     y     z
#>    <dbl> <dbl> <ord>     <ord> <ord>   <dbl> <dbl> <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#>  1  506.  0.23 Ideal     E     SI2      61.5    55   326  3.95  3.98  2.43
#>  2  506.  0.21 Premium   E     SI1      59.8    61   326  3.89  3.84  2.31
```

title: Neural network support: normalization layers (BatchNorm, LayerNorm)
description:
Follow-on from #149. Milestones 1-3 of the neural network support work (bare torch, `parsnip::mlp(engine = "brulee")`, and bare keras3 `Sequential`, all feed-forward and fully-connected) are merged. This tracks Milestone 4 from the dev plan: support for `BatchNorm`/`LayerNorm` layers, which real deep MLPs commonly interleave between `Linear` and activation, and which the current walkers error on outright.

## Scope

- **BatchNorm** (`torch::nn_batch_norm1d`, keras `layer_batch_normalization()`): at eval time this is a fixed per-channel affine transform (`(x - running_mean) / sqrt(running_var + eps) * gamma + beta`), read directly off the layer's stored parameters (`running_mean`/`running_var`/`weight`/`bias` for torch; `moving_mean`/`moving_variance`/`gamma`/`beta` for keras). Implement as another cheap layer in the walk first (one column per channel, same generator as everything else); algebraic folding into the preceding `Linear` layer's weight/bias is a possible follow-up optimization, not required initially.
- Epsilon must be read from each fitted layer's own config, never hardcoded (torch defaults to `1e-5`, keras to `1e-3`).
- **LayerNorm**: computes a row-wise mean/variance over the layer's own already-generated neuron columns at inference time (no fixed running stats to read off the fitted object). Real new logic, not a copy of the BatchNorm translator, but still row-local arithmetic (no window functions or cross-row aggregation needed).
- Tests: extend the existing torch/brulee/keras3 test networks with a BatchNorm-containing variant and a LayerNorm-containing variant, same predict()-matches-original structure as the existing tests.

**Size:** M. **Risk:** Low for BatchNorm, Low-Medium for LayerNorm.

title: orbital disagrees with tidypredict_fit() for aorsf regression forests
description:
Separate from the upstream discrepancy in tidymodels/tidypredict#439, orbital's own output does not match the expression it is translating.

orbital should be an exact restatement of `tidypredict_fit()`, so any nonzero gap here is orbital's, independent of whether tidypredict agrees with aorsf.

```r
library(parsnip)
library(bonsai)
set.seed(123)

d <- modeldata::ames[, c("Sale_Price", "Lot_Area", "Gr_Liv_Area", "Year_Built", "Full_Bath")]
d$Sale_Price <- log10(d$Sale_Price)

f <- fit(rand_forest(mode = "regression", engine = "aorsf", trees = 20), Sale_Price ~ ., d)

own <- predict(f, d)$.pred
tp  <- tidypredict::tidypredict_to_column(d, f$fit)$fit
orb <- predict(orbital(f), d)$.pred

max(abs(orb - tp))
#> [1] 0.02403107   <- orbital vs the expression it translates
max(abs(own - tp))
#> [1] 0.04904059   <- upstream, tidymodels/tidypredict#439
max(abs(orb - own))
#> [1] 0.05238703
```

The outcome spans 4.11 to 5.88, so 0.024 is structural rather than floating-point noise.

A likely place to look: aorsf wraps its mean in an `NA` guard rather than combining trees as a plain sum or mean, and `format_separate_trees()` assumes the plain form. That is a guess, not a diagnosis.

aorsf 0.1.6, tidypredict 1.1.1.9000.

aorsf support is blocked on both this and #439.

title: print() corrupts numeric literals: pretty_print() uses sub() without fixed = TRUE
description:
`pretty_print()` uses `sub()` without `fixed = TRUE`, so numeric literals in the print method are treated as regular expressions. When one equation contains a threshold like `0.5`, that pattern means `0`-anychar-`5` and matches digit runs inside *other* equations, silently corrupting the coefficients shown on screen.

Display only: the stored expressions, the generated SQL, `orbital_json_write()` output, and all predictions are correct. But the corrupted output looks like a plausible number rather than obvious garbage, which makes it easy to misread a coefficient.

## Reproducible example

Minimal, no modelling involved:

```r
library(orbital)

x <- c(a = "2.025899", b = "0.5")
class(x) <- "orbital_class"
attr(x, "pred_names") <- "b"

print(x)
#> ── orbital Object ──────────────────────────────────────────────
#> • a = 2.0.5899
#> • b = 0.5
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> 2 equations in total.
```

`a` should print as `2.025899`.

Through the normal API, any classification object that includes a `.pred_class` equation triggers it, because the `case_when()` threshold supplies the `0.5`:

```r
library(orbital)
library(recipes)
library(parsnip)
library(workflows)

data(two_class_dat, package = "modeldata")

rec <- recipe(Class ~ ., data = two_class_dat) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

fit_obj <- fit(workflow(rec, logistic_reg()), data = two_class_dat)
ob <- orbital(fit_obj, type = c("class", "prob"))

unclass(ob)[["A"]]
#> [1] "(A - 2.0258990341433103) / 0.89745306486446397"

print(ob)
#> ── orbital Object ──────────────────────────────────────────────
#> • A = (A - 2.0.5899) / 0.8974531
#> • B = (B - 1.540.52) / 0.7304615
#> • .pred_class = dplyr::case_when(1 - 1/(1 + exp(-0.3490777 + (A * -1.1062 ...
#> • .pred_Class1 = 1 - (1 - 1/(1 + exp(-0.3490777 + (A * -1.106265) + (B * ...
#> • .pred_Class2 = 1 - `.pred_Class1`
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> 5 equations in total.
```

`A` should print `(A - 2.025899) / 0.8974531`. Note `B` is hit too: the pattern matches `035` inside `1.540352`.

Asking for `type = "prob"` alone prints correctly, since there is no `0.5` anywhere in the object. That is why this doesn't show up in regression examples.

## Cause

In `pretty_print()` (R/orbital.R):

```r
for (i in seq_along(old_values)) {
  x <- sub(old_values[i], new_values[i], x)
}
```

`old_values[i]` is a regex, not a literal:

```r
sub("0.5", "0.5", "2.025899")                # "2.0.5899"
sub("0.5", "0.5", "2.025899", fixed = TRUE)  # "2.025899"
```

The replacement inserts a literal `.`, which is why the result reads as a decimal number.

Two things make it worse than a single bad match:

1. `old_values` is `unlist()`ed across all equations, so a number from equation 3 is substituted into equations 1 and 2.
2. `sub()` is applied to the whole vector `x` rather than element-wise, so the leak is silent and affects unrelated equations.

## Suggested fix

`fixed = TRUE` is enough to fix the corruption. Doing it element-wise via `regmatches<-` also removes the cross-equation leakage and drops the loop:

```r
pretty_print <- function(x, digits = 7) {
  vapply(
    x,
    function(eq) {
      m <- gregexpr("[0-9]+\\.?[0-9]+", eq)
      nums <- regmatches(eq, m)[[1]]
      if (!length(nums)) {
        return(eq)
      }
      regmatches(eq, m) <- list(as.character(signif(as.numeric(nums), digits)))
      eq
    },
    character(1),
    USE.NAMES = FALSE
  )
}
```

Gives `"(A - 2.025899) / 0.8974531"` and `"(B - 1.540352) / 0.7304615"`.

A regression test along the lines of `expect_equal(pretty_print(c("2.025899", "0.5")), c("2.025899", "0.5"))` would pin it.

## Two minor things in the same function

Neither changes a value, so feel free to ignore:

- `1.23456789e-05` prints as `1.234568e-5` (the `05` exponent is matched and rounded to `5`).
- The pattern `[0-9]+\\.?[0-9]+` requires two or more digits, so a bare `5` is never rounded. Presumably `[0-9]+(\\.[0-9]+)?` was intended.

## Versions

Reproduced on orbital 0.5.1.9000 and confirmed present in the CRAN 0.5.1 sources (the function is identical in both).

Introduced by the signif printing added in #4.

title: Split up longer expressions into multiple lines
Use digits17 control for all numeric serialization
description:
## Summary

Ensure `deparse1(e, control = "digits17")` is used consistently everywhere orbital serializes numeric values to SQL strings.

## Why This Matters

IEEE 754 double-precision floats require **up to 17 significant decimal digits** to guarantee a unique round-trip representation. Without this:

```r
x <- 0.123456789012345678
deparse(x)                        # "0.123456789012346" (loses precision)
deparse1(x, control = "digits17") # "0.12345678901234568" (full precision)
```

## Database Implications

1. **Reproducibility**: Users expect `predict(model, new_data)` in R to match database-side predictions exactly. Precision loss breaks this contract.

2. **Numerical stability**: Coefficients from regularized models (glmnet, etc.) or normalized features can have many significant digits. Truncation introduces bias that compounds across operations.

3. **Comparison testing**: Without full precision, unit tests comparing R vs SQL outputs will show floating-point drift.

## Scope

Apply `digits17` anywhere numeric values are serialized:
- Model coefficients
- Preprocessing parameters (means, SDs, normalization bounds)
- Any numeric literals in generated expressions

---

```r
GRID_SIZE <- 10

data(penguins, package = "modeldata")

penguins_fold <- vfold_cv(penguins_train, v  = 3)
plan(multisession)

rec_spec <-
  recipe(body_mass_g ~ ., data = penguins_train) |>
  step_unknown(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_nzv(all_predictors()) |>
  step_scale(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_center(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_corr(all_predictors(), threshold = 0.5)

  set_mode("regression") |>
  set_engine("glm")
glm_res <- workflow(rec_spec, glm_spec) |> 
  tune_grid(penguins_fold, control = control_stack_grid(), grid = GRID_SIZE)
```

title: Factor variables treated as character in impute_mode recipe step
description:
## The problem

If you have a factor variable and use `step_impute_mode()`, the formula generated treats it as a character variable. In the example below, cyl is made into a factor but on the impute step of the formula, the following line is generated:

`#> • cyl = dplyr::if_else(is.na(cyl), "8", cyl)`

Perhaps this should instead be generated as one of the following:

- `cyl = dplyr::if_else(is.na(cyl), 8, cyl)`
- `cyl = dplyr::if_else(is.na(cyl), "8", as.character(cyl))`

## Reproducible example

``` r
library(orbital)
library(tidymodels)

mtcars_f <- mtcars |>
  dplyr::mutate(cyl=as.factor(cyl))

rec_spec <- recipe(mpg ~ ., data = mtcars_f) |>
  step_impute_mode(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

lm_spec <- linear_reg()

wf_spec <- workflow(rec_spec, lm_spec)

wf_fit <- fit(wf_spec, mtcars_f)

orbital_obj <- orbital(wf_fit)

orbital_obj
```

description:

```{r}
! Is not implemented for a <last_fit> object.
```

This {orbital} implementation would be excellent, and I'm loving this early stage package! 🚀

- Will any {embed} functions be implemented with this? For example, `embed::step_lencode_mixed()` or `embed::step_lencode_glm()` (although, I fully recognize this would be a bear) 🙏
